title: Tennis IQ Question Bank
source: Source-reviewed question bank. Per-question evidence, corrections and limitations: docs/audit/final-ledger.json and docs/QUESTION_AUDIT.md.

questions.question: How long is a regulation tennis court from baseline to baseline?
questions.explain: ITF Rule 1: the court is a rectangle 78 feet (23.77 m) long. That length is the same for singles and doubles.

questions.question: How wide is a singles court?
questions.explain: Singles is 27 feet (8.23 m) wide. Doubles expands to 36 feet (10.97 m).

questions.question: How wide is a doubles court?
questions.explain: Doubles is 36 feet (10.97 m) wide. Each alley adds 4.5 feet (1.37 m) on a side.

questions.question: How wide is each doubles alley?
questions.explain: 36 − 27 = 9 feet of extra width, split equally: 4.5 feet (1.37 m) per side.

questions.question: How high is the net at the center strap?
choices: 42 inches at both posts and center
questions.explain: The net must be 3 feet (0.914 m) at the center, held down by a white strap.

questions.question: How high is the net at the posts?
questions.explain: The net is supported at 3 feet 6 inches (1.07 m) at the posts and held at 3 feet (0.914 m) in the center. Posts may extend no more than 1 inch above the net cord.

questions.question: How far is the service line from the net?
questions.explain: Service boxes are 21 feet (6.40 m) deep. Baseline to net is 39 feet, so the backcourt behind the service line is 18 feet.

questions.question: Where are the net posts placed on a doubles court?
questions.explain: The centre of each post is 3 feet (0.914 m) outside the doubles court.

questions.question: You are playing singles on a doubles net. What extra piece of equipment makes the net legal?
questions.explain: Singles sticks support the net at 3 ft 6 in at a point 3 feet outside each singles sideline so the net is not sagging too low at the singles edges.

questions.question: A ball lands on the outer edge of the baseline. The call is…
choices: Out — only the inside of the line counts
In — lines are part of the court
Out if it hits the line after the bounce
questions.explain: Lines are in. Measurements are taken to the outside of the lines.

questions.question: Which line is allowed to be the widest?
questions.explain: ITF Rule 1 permits baselines up to 4 inches (10 cm) wide. Other lines are 1–2 inches, with the center service line and center mark exactly 2 inches wide.

questions.question: From baseline to net on one side of the court is…
questions.explain: Half of 78 feet is 39 feet (11.89 m).

questions.question: What colours are permitted for standard adult tennis balls under ITF Appendix I?
questions.explain: ITF: white or yellow, uniform fabric cover, stitchless seams. Yellow won because TV cameras could see it.

questions.question: A Type 2 (standard) tennis ball must weigh…
questions.explain: Mass window is 56.0–59.4 g (1.975–2.095 oz) for adult Type 1, 2, 3, and high-altitude balls.

questions.question: In the official bounce test, the ball is dropped from…
questions.explain: The rebound test drops the ball from 254 cm (100 inches) onto a smooth, rigid, horizontal surface of high mass. A standard Type 2 ball must rebound within 135–147 cm (53–58 inches).

questions.question: Maximum legal racket length is…
questions.explain: ITF Appendix II limits overall racket length to 73.7 cm (29.0 inches). The common 27-inch adult racket length is not the maximum.

questions.question: Type 3 (slow) balls differ from Type 2 mainly because they are…
questions.explain: Type 3 diameter is 7.00–7.30 cm versus 6.54–6.86 cm for Type 2. They are used to slow the game on fast courts or at altitude in some settings.

questions.question: Why were yellow balls adopted for elite play?
questions.explain: ITF approved yellow in 1972 after research showed yellow was easier to track on colour TV. Wimbledon kept white balls until 1986.

questions.question: What does “love” mean?
questions.explain: Under ITF Rule 5, a player with no points has a score of love.

questions.question: The point names in a game go…
questions.explain: ITF Rule 5 uses love, 15, 30 and 40. At 40–40 the score is deuce, and a two-point margin is needed to win a standard advantage game.

questions.question: 40–40 is called…
questions.explain: Deuce. From there you need two consecutive points. The next point is advantage; lose it and you return to deuce.

questions.question: Whose score is spoken first?
choices: The player who won the last point
questions.explain: Always server first: “30–15” means the server has 30.

questions.question: Standard set: first to how many games, by how many?
questions.explain: Six games with a two-game margin (6–4, 6–3, 7–5). At 6–6 you usually play a tiebreak.

questions.question: A standard set tiebreak is first to…
questions.explain: First to 7, must win by 2. 7–5 wins; 7–6 does not — play on to 8–6, 9–7, and so on.

questions.question: Since 2022, a Grand Slam singles main-draw deciding set at 6–6 is decided by…
questions.explain: All four majors use a first-to-10, win-by-two tiebreak at 6–6 in a singles deciding set.

questions.question: Under standard tiebreak end-change rules, when do players first change ends?
questions.explain: Players change ends after every six points, first after point six; for example, at 3–3, 4–2, or 5–1.

questions.question: Tiebreak serve order starts…
choices: Two serves each from the first ball
questions.explain: The player due to serve starts with one point, then each player serves two points until the breaker ends.

questions.question: Men’s singles main-draw matches at Grand Slam tournaments are played in which format?
questions.explain: The Grand Slam rulebook prescribes best-of-five for men’s singles main-draw matches. Women’s singles main-draw matches use best-of-three.

questions.question: No-ad scoring means…
choices: At deuce, one deciding point is played
questions.explain: At deuce, one deciding point wins the game. In singles and same-gender doubles, the receiving side chooses the receiving court. In mixed doubles, the receiver must be the same gender as the server; receiving positions are not changed for that point.

questions.question: A 10-point “match tiebreak” is most often used to…
choices: Replace a deciding set in doubles
questions.explain: Many doubles events play two sets then a 10-point breaker instead of a full third set.

questions.question: If the score in games is 6–6 and there is no tiebreak, what kind of set is being played?
questions.explain: An advantage set continues until one player leads by two games. Final-set advantage sets used to be common at Roland-Garros and Wimbledon.

questions.question: “Ad-in” means…
choices: The next game starts on the ad side
questions.explain: Ad-in = advantage server. Ad-out = advantage receiver.

questions.question: The serve must land…
choices: In the service box directly in front of the server
In the service box diagonally opposite
Past the service line on the full court
questions.explain: Diagonal serve into the correct box. Start each game from the deuce court (server’s right).

questions.question: Under the standard service-let rule, a serve clips the net and lands in the correct service box. What is the call?
questions.explain: Service let: replay the same serve. A let on second serve does not give first serve back.

questions.question: Two faults on the same point is…
choices: A double fault — point to the receiver
questions.explain: Double fault loses the point.

questions.question: Which of these is a foot fault?
choices: Jumping off the ground as you hit the serve
Small foot adjustment before the toss
Touching the baseline with a foot before contact
Standing more than two metres behind the baseline
questions.explain: Jumping is legal. Walking/running to a new spot is not. Touching the baseline or court before contact is a foot fault.

questions.question: You miss the ball completely on a serve swing. The call is…
choices: Replay with no fault if it was first serve
questions.explain: A whiff on the serve is a fault. (If you abort the motion and do not swing, you may start again.)

questions.question: A serve hits a singles stick and then lands in the correct box. It is…
questions.explain: ITF: a serve that hits a permanent fixture, singles stick, or net post before bouncing is a fault.

questions.question: Players change ends in a normal set…
choices: After the 1st, 3rd, and every subsequent odd game
questions.explain: Odd games: 1, 3, 5… So after 1, then after 3 (score 2–1), and so on.

questions.question: Who has the first choice of serving, receiving, selecting an end, or asking the opponent to choose before a match?
choices: The winner of the toss (or the player who wins the spin)
questions.explain: The toss winner may choose serve/receive, choose an end, or require the opponent to choose. The opponent makes the remaining choice under ITF Rule 9.

questions.question: A ball rolls onto your court mid-rally and a let is called. The server had already faulted once. What happens?
choices: Whole point replayed — first serve restored
questions.explain: A general let (not a second-serve service let) replays the entire point, so first serve is restored.

questions.question: Can you reach over the net to play a ball?
choices: Yes, if the ball has already bounced on your side and spin/wind carries it back
Yes, at any time as long as you don’t touch the net
questions.explain: You must let it cross to your side first, with the classic exception that a ball that bounces in your court and then goes back may be followed over.

questions.question: Who patented boxed lawn-tennis sets in 1874 under the name Sphairistikè?
questions.explain: Wingfield commercialised lawn tennis. The first club, however, was already forming in Leamington in 1872 around Harry Gem.

questions.question: The first Wimbledon Championship was held in…
questions.explain: 1877 at the All England Croquet and Lawn Tennis Club. Spencer Gore won the gentlemen’s singles.

questions.question: What shape was Wingfield’s original patented court?
questions.explain: The 1874 court narrowed at the net. Wimbledon 1877 switched to the rectangle still used today.

questions.question: The most cited etymology of the word “tennis” is…
choices: French tenez, “take/receive,” called before the serve
A village named Tennis in Wales
questions.explain: Players of jeu de paume are said to have warned the opponent with tenez.

questions.question: The Open Era — professionals allowed into the majors — begins in…
questions.explain: 1968. That is the B.C./A.D. line for modern prize-money tennis.

questions.question: Who is credited with popularising the tiebreak that stopped endless advantage sets?
questions.explain: Van Alen’s VASSS ideas led to the tiebreak. The US Open used early versions from 1970.

questions.question: Davis Cup began in 1900 as a challenge between…
choices: the United States and Great Britain
questions.explain: Dwight Davis put up the punchbowl. USA vs British Isles.

questions.question: Which scoring features did the MCC’s 1876 lawn-tennis rule revision adopt from real tennis?
questions.explain: The ITF’s history records that the MCC’s 1876 revisions adopted real tennis scoring with deuce and advantage and allowed two serves.

questions.question: Lawn tennis grew out of which older indoor game?
questions.explain: Real tennis / jeu de paume contributed scoring language, the net, and the culture. Lawn tennis moved it outdoors onto grass.

questions.question: Tennis was part of the first modern Olympics in…
questions.explain: Tennis was an 1896 sport, later dropped, then restored as a full medal sport in 1988 — the year Graf completed the Golden Slam.

questions.question: Which Grand Slam is played on clay?
questions.explain: Roland-Garros (French Open) is the clay major. Wimbledon is grass. AO and US Open are hard.

questions.question: Which Grand Slam is still played on grass?
questions.explain: Wimbledon is the only major on grass. Queen’s and Halle are important grass tune-ups, not Slams.

questions.question: In the normal modern calendar, what is the order of the four majors?
questions.explain: January hard in Melbourne, late May clay in Paris, June/July grass in London, August/September hard in New York.

questions.question: A calendar-year Grand Slam means…
choices: Winning any four titles in a year
Winning all four majors in the same year
Winning three majors and the Tour Finals
Holding all four titles at once across two years
questions.explain: Same calendar year. Holding all four at once across two seasons is a non-calendar-year Slam.

questions.question: Who is the only man with two calendar Grand Slams, including the only Open Era one?
questions.explain: Laver in 1962 (amateur) and 1969 (Open Era). Budge did it once, in 1938.

questions.question: Who won all four women’s singles majors and Olympic singles gold in 1988?
questions.explain: Steffi Graf completed this calendar Golden Slam in 1988.

questions.question: At the end of 2025, which man held the most Grand Slam singles titles, excluding wheelchair events?
questions.explain: At that cutoff, Djokovic had 24 major singles titles, Nadal 22 and Federer 20.

questions.question: Who has won the most Roland-Garros men’s singles titles?
questions.explain: Rafael Nadal won 14 Roland-Garros men’s singles titles from 2005 through 2022.

questions.question: Through the 2025 Championships, who held the Open Era record for Wimbledon men’s singles titles?
questions.explain: Federer 8. Sampras 7, Djokovic 7.

questions.question: At the end of 2025, who held the women’s Grand Slam singles title record across amateur and Open Eras, excluding wheelchair events?
questions.explain: Margaret Court won 24: 13 before the Open Era and 11 during it.

questions.question: The longest tennis match: Isner vs Mahut at Wimbledon 2010. The final set was…
questions.explain: Isner won the fifth set 70–68. The first-round match took 11 hours 5 minutes over three days.

questions.question: Through the end of 2025, which was the longest Grand Slam singles final by playing time?
questions.explain: 5 hours 53 minutes. Isner–Mahut was longer but it was a first-round match, not a final.

questions.question: The US Open surface timeline is…
questions.explain: Grass through 1974, clay 1975–77, hard from 1978. Connors won it on all three.

questions.question: Wimbledon’s clothing rule requires players to wear…
choices: Almost entirely white — not cream or off-white
Club colours of the All England Club
questions.explain: Players wear almost entirely white, with limited trim under the detailed rules. Since 2023, female players may wear mid/dark undershorts no longer than their shorts or skirt.

questions.question: Under the 2026 ATP singles ranking table, how many points does a Grand Slam champion earn?
questions.explain: 2000 for the title. Runner-up 1300 on the ATP table.

questions.question: An ace is…
choices: A legal serve the receiver does not touch
A serve that hits the line
questions.explain: Untouched. If the receiver gets strings on it and still fails, that is a service winner, not an ace.

questions.question: A bagel is a set won…
questions.explain: Zero looks like a bagel. 6–1 is a breadstick.

questions.question: Break point means…
choices: The server is one point from the game
The receiver is one point from winning the server’s game
The set is one game from ending

questions.question: No-man’s land is…
choices: The area between service line and baseline
questions.explain: Too far back to finish at net, too far forward to cover a deep ball comfortably. Live there and you get passed or jammed.

questions.question: An inside-out forehand is hit…
choices: From the forehand corner down the line
By running around a backhand and driving the forehand crosscourt
As a squash shot off a wide ball
questions.explain: A right-handed player runs around the backhand side and hits a forehand diagonally toward the opposing ad court. That is a right-handed opponent’s backhand side, but a left-hander’s forehand side.

questions.question: A moonball is…
choices: A very high, looping, usually heavy ball used to reset or push someone back
A smash from the service line
A drop shot that bounces twice
questions.explain: A moonball is a high, looping groundstroke, usually with topspin and depth. It can push the opponent back and change the rally’s rhythm.

questions.question: To “hold” is to…
questions.explain: Hold serve. The other side of the coin is a break.

questions.question: Wrong-footing an opponent means…
choices: Hitting behind them after they have committed the other way
Making them serve from the ad court
questions.explain: Wrong-footing means sending the ball behind an opponent who has already committed to moving the other way.

questions.question: A walkover is awarded when…
choices: The opponent cannot start the match
A code violation ends the match
questions.explain: Didn’t start = walkover. Started and stopped = retirement.

questions.question: The deuce court is…
choices: The left side from the server’s view
The right side from the server’s view as a game begins
questions.explain: Even points (0–0, 15–15, 30–30, deuce) are played from the deuce/right court.

questions.question: Why is crosscourt the percentage rally ball?
choices: The net is higher in the middle
The diagonal is longer and the net is lower in the middle
You cannot hit an inside-out shot down the line
questions.explain: The full singles-court diagonal is about 82.5 feet, versus 78 feet along a sideline. A crosscourt ball also travels over the lower central part of the net. These margins often make it a safer rally direction.

questions.question: “Serve + 1” means…
choices: Serving and immediately volleying every point
Planning the serve target and the next ball as one pattern
Hitting an ace plus a winner
questions.explain: Most tour points die in one to four shots. The first ball after the serve is where matches are designed.

questions.question: After a wide deuce-court serve pulls the returner off court and produces an attackable return, which common serve-plus-one pattern uses the open space?
choices: Another ball behind them into the same deuce corner
An attacking ball into the open ad-court space
questions.explain: One common pattern is wide serve, then attack the open court. Return quality and the opponent’s recovery can make another target preferable.

questions.question: On clay, the high-percentage plan is usually…
choices: Height, shape, depth, and constructing a short ball
questions.explain: Clay is slow and high. You win by moving people and forcing the error or the short ball, not by ending every point on shot two.

questions.question: On grass, the surface tends to…
choices: Sit up high and reward long rallies
Stay low and take time away, rewarding first strike
questions.explain: Low, sometimes skiddy bounce. First-strike tennis and a real volley when the ball sits up short.

questions.question: Approaching down the middle is underrated because…
choices: It shrinks passing angles and avoids giving a short-angle look
It is required by the rules
It opens both alleys on purpose
questions.explain: A wide approach looks pretty and gives the passer two big windows. A deep heavy approach through the middle can be the smarter close.

questions.question: Why do sharp angles get easier as you move forward?
choices: The ball is slower near the net
Geometry: closer to the net, the available cone of legal targets widens
The alleys count in singles if you are at net
Spin stops working from the back
questions.explain: From five metres behind the baseline many “angle” attempts are just long crosscourts or balls in the net.

questions.question: A second serve is usually…
choices: Faster than the first, aimed at the lines
Higher-margin: kick or slice, often at the body or backhand
questions.explain: The tax on a miss is the point. Shape and a target that jams the returner beat hero flat seconds.

questions.question: In Craig O’Shannessy’s published Brain Game rally-length breakdown, approximately what share of points fall in the 0–4-shot category?
questions.explain: That published breakdown gives roughly 70% to 0–4 shots. It is a coaching benchmark, not a fixed percentage for every match or level.

questions.question: After you hit a wide crosscourt, you should recover…
choices: To the exact centre hash every time
Toward a position that covers the opponent’s reply angles, usually short of the centre mark after a wide crosscourt
All the way to the opposite alley
questions.explain: After a wide crosscourt from the baseline, recover toward the middle while shading toward the likely crosscourt reply. The best position changes with the opponent’s contact point and available angles.

questions.question: ATP / WTA rankings are based on…
choices: A rolling 52-week points total from a capped number of results
questions.explain: ATP and WTA rankings generally use a rolling 52-week period, with rules limiting which results count. Special expiry and mandatory-result rules can apply.

questions.question: An ATP Masters 1000 winner earns…
questions.explain: The “1000” is the title points. Slams are 2000.

questions.question: On the 2026 ATP calendar, which surface is used at both Indian Wells and Miami?
questions.explain: The official ATP calendar lists Indian Wells and Miami as hard-court Masters 1000 events.

questions.question: In the classic Hawk-Eye challenge system, a player typically starts each set with…
questions.explain: Keep the challenge if you are right; lose one if you are wrong. Many events later switched to fully automated line calling.

questions.question: Yellow tennis balls were approved by the ITF in 1972. When did Wimbledon switch from white balls?
questions.explain: Wimbledon held out until 1986. A classic quiz trap.

questions.question: Jimmy Connors is unique at the US Open because he…
choices: Won it on grass, clay, and hard
questions.explain: The Open’s surface hopping made that possible. Nobody else has the three-surface US Open set.

questions.question: Topspin makes a ball…
choices: Stay in the air longer and skid
Dive down after clearing the net, allowing a higher net clearance with a still-in landing
questions.explain: Magnus effect: topspin curves the flight downward. That is why heavy-forehand players can swing hard and still land the ball.

questions.question: A sliced backhand typically…
choices: Kicks up high after the bounce
Floats with backspin and stays lower
Must bounce twice to be legal
Cannot be used as an approach
questions.explain: Backspin + low net clearance = a skidding or floating ball that stays down. Excellent change-up and approach.

questions.question: Why does the rulebook insist the net is lower in the middle?
choices: It is just sag from poor tension
It is specified: 3 ft centre, 3 ft 6 in posts, which makes the middle the higher-percentage crossing point
questions.explain: Attacking through the middle has a lower barrier. Wide balls face a higher net — one reason sharp crosscourt passing shots are harder than they look.

questions.question: If you are not sure whether a ball was out, The Code says…

questions.question: You call a ball out, then realize it was good. What happens?

questions.explain: The Code §12 exception: reversing a fault call on a net-cord first serve restores first serve.

questions.question: In doubles, partners disagree — one says out, one says good. The call is…
questions.explain: The Code §14: give opponents the call that most benefits them. Out + good = good.

questions.question: May you ask a spectator to confirm a line call?
choices: Yes, if they had a better angle
questions.explain: The Code §16.

questions.question: You see a ball rolling on from the next court, keep playing a sitters put-away, miss it, then claim a let. Valid?
choices: No — you took the two-chance option and forfeited the let
Only if it was match point
questions.explain: The Code §17: prompt calls. If you choose to play the ball, you do not get a second chance.

questions.question: A stray ball rolls on mid-point. Who may call a let?
choices: Any player on the affected court, promptly
questions.explain: The Code §18. Delay unreasonably and you lose the right to the let.

questions.question: The ball hits you before bouncing. You…
choices: Play on if you were standing out
questions.explain: The Code §19 and §43: a ball in play that touches you, or that you catch before the bounce, is your point lost — wherever you are standing.

questions.question: You reach over and hit the ball before it crosses the net. Result?
questions.explain: The Code §19: hitting the ball before it crosses the net loses the point.

questions.question: On clay, if any part of the ball mark touches the line…
choices: Inspect from the other side of the net
questions.explain: The Code §21. Opponent shall not cross the net to inspect the mark. You are not required to show the mark.

questions.question: Who may call a foot fault in an unofficiated match?
choices: Receiver or receiver’s partner — only after warning and trying to get an official, and only if flagrant
questions.explain: The Code §24. Touching the line is still a foot fault (§23) even if you do not follow the serve to net.

questions.question: In doubles, who typically calls the service line on return?
questions.explain: The Code §25: partner takes the service line; receiver takes sideline and center service line. Either may call a ball they clearly see.

questions.question: May the serving team call a first serve out?
choices: Generally no — the receiver may be giving benefit of the doubt. Exception if the receiver plays a fault and does not put it in play
questions.explain: The Code §26. Serving team must call out a second serve they clearly see out.

questions.question: Who may call a service let?
choices: Any player, promptly, before the return goes out or is hit by the serving team
questions.explain: The Code §27 permits any player to call a service let before the return goes out of play or is hit by the server or partner. For an apparent or near ace, the call must be prompt.

questions.question: If you swing at a serve, The Code treats you as…
questions.explain: The Code §29: attempt to return = presumed ready, even on a quick serve. You may not then become unready except for outside interference.

questions.question: A ball rolls on and interrupts the second-serve motion. The server gets…
questions.explain: The Code §30: interrupted second-serve motion because a ball came on = two serves. Brief clearing between serves is not automatically two serves unless the delay is a real interruption. Receiver judges that.

questions.question: The server caused a delay between first and second serve. The server gets…
questions.explain: The Code §30: server caused the delay → one serve. Receiver or outside interference → two serves.

questions.question: Who announces the score in an unofficiated match?
choices: The server — game score before the first point, point score before each later point
questions.explain: The Code §31.

questions.question: Score dispute first preference under The Code is…
choices: Count agreed points/games and replay only the disputed ones
questions.explain: The Code §32. Then mutually agreeable score, then spin a racket / toss a coin. Coin toss also if you cannot agree who served a disputed game or tiebreak point.

questions.question: Talking in doubles while the ball is coming toward your team is…
questions.explain: The Code §34: partners may talk when the ball is moving toward them. Do not talk when it is going toward the opponents. Singles: do not talk during points.

questions.question: You yell “get back” on a weak lob and it distracts the opponent about to hit. If they stop immediately they may claim…
questions.explain: The Code §34 example. If they play the lob and miss, they lost the right to claim by not stopping in time.

questions.question: A player yells after a bee sting during a point. That is…
choices: Unintentional hindrance — opponent may claim a let
questions.explain: The Code §34.

questions.question: May you feint with your body during a point?
choices: Yes. Waving the arms or stamping only to distract is not allowed
questions.explain: The Code §35. You may also change position during the toss. Distraction-only movement or sound is illegal.

questions.question: Your racket flies out of your hand mid-point. You may claim a let?
choices: No — something within your control is not a let
Only if it hits the net
questions.explain: The Code §36. Same for a shoe coming off or tripping on your own hat. Opponent may call a let if your hat falls off and hinders them.

questions.question: Opponent’s cell phone rings during a point. You may…
choices: Only ask them to silence it after the game
Stop immediately and claim the point — ringing phone is a deliberate hindrance
questions.explain: The Code §36.

questions.question: Who may rule that grunting is a hindrance?
choices: The opponent, immediately taking the point
Only an official, after the process in The Code
questions.explain: The Code §37 reserves grunting-hindrance rulings to officials. The official orders a let or loss of point depending on whether the player was previously warned.

questions.question: Server’s racket accidentally hits the receiver, who cannot continue in time. Match result?
questions.explain: The Code §38: accidental injury — injured player suffers the consequence (retirement). Deliberate injury — default against the offender.

questions.question: Warm-up under The Code is…
choices: Five to ten minutes, hitting to the opponent, not a practice session
questions.explain: The Code §3–4. Take warm-up serves before the first serve of the match. Decline to warm the opponent up and you forfeit your own warm-up.

questions.question: Points played in good faith…
choices: Are replayed if the net was the wrong height
Stand, even if you later find the net was four inches high or you served from the wrong side
questions.explain: The Code §2. Fix the condition after the point.

questions.question: Handshake at the end of a match means…
choices: Acknowledgment that the match is over
questions.explain: The Code §2.

questions.question: Towels belong…
choices: On the ground outside the net post or at the back fence — never on the net
questions.explain: The Code §46.

questions.question: Catching a ball in play before it bounces…
choices: Wins the point if you were standing out
Loses the point regardless of where you stand
questions.explain: The Code §43.

questions.question: Changeover time that becomes stalling if exceeded (The Code)…
choices: 90 seconds on the odd-game changeover; 2 minutes on the set break
questions.explain: The Code §40. Also: over-long warm-up, playing at one-third pace, starting an argument to rest, clearing a first serve that does not need clearing, excessive bouncing.

questions.question: The server asks for a third ball that is sitting right there. The receiver…
choices: Must comply when the third ball is readily available
questions.explain: The Code §22. Distant balls wait until the end of the game.

questions.question: All points in a match, including match point, are…
choices: Called more generously for the trailer
questions.explain: The Code §10.

questions.question: You ask the opponent if a ball was out. They say it was good. You must…
questions.explain: The Code §11. If neither has an opinion, the ball is good. You only ask on a call that ended the point.

questions.question: Should you call your own shots out if you clearly see them out?
questions.explain: The Code §13. Exception: first serve.

questions.question: Broken racket mid-match: you may leave to replace it, but…
choices: You are on the Point Penalty System for delay
questions.explain: The Code §45. Clothing/equipment other than a racket that fails outside your control: reasonable suspension after the point.

questions.question: Where do singles sticks go (USTA Comment)?
choices: Center of each stick 3 feet outside the outer edge of the singles sideline, diagonally opposite
questions.explain: USTA Comment 1.2 in Friend at Court.

questions.question: Tied point scores other than deuce are announced…
questions.explain: USTA scoring language: 15-all, 30-all; 40-40 is deuce.

questions.question: A 2026 ITF/FAC clarification on Rule 18 Case 1 concerned…
choices: Where the server may stand in doubles for a foot fault
questions.explain: 2026 Friend at Court summary of changes: Rule 18, Case 1, doubles stance.

questions.question: If you discover after a point that you served from the wrong half…
choices: The point stands; correct it before the next point
questions.explain: The Code §2: points played in good faith stand.

questions.question: Underhand serves in USTA play are…
choices: Legal if the serve otherwise meets the rules
questions.explain: ITF/USTA: the serve must be hit before it hits the ground; underhand is allowed.

questions.question: In USTA League matches without officials, you follow…
choices: Friend at Court, including The Code
questions.explain: League regs incorporate Friend at Court and The Code.

questions.question: NTRP in USTA League is…
choices: A national ranking points total like ATP
A skill rating used to form fairly matched teams
questions.explain: National Tennis Rating Program. Separate from ATP/WTA computer rankings.

questions.question: Wimbledon first staged a ladies’ singles championship in…
questions.explain: 1884. Maud Watson beat her sister Lilian in the first final, 6–8, 6–3, 6–3. Thirteen players entered. Prize: a silver flower basket worth 20 guineas.

questions.question: Who won the first Wimbledon ladies’ singles title?
questions.explain: Maud Watson, 19, in 1884. She defended in 1885.

questions.question: As recorded in Wimbledon’s 2022 compendium, who was its youngest ladies’ singles champion?
questions.explain: Lottie Dod won in 1887 at 15 years and 285 days.

questions.question: The Australian Championships added a women’s singles event in…
questions.explain: 1922. The men’s event dates to 1905.

questions.question: Suzanne Lenglen’s Wimbledon singles titles total…
questions.explain: Six (1919–23, 1925). She turned professional in 1926 and never played Helen Wills again after their only meeting at Cannes.

questions.question: Helen Wills Moody’s 19 major singles titles split as…
choices: 8 Wimbledon, 7 US, 4 French — she never won Australia
questions.explain: Helen Wills won eight Wimbledon, seven US and four French singles championships, for 19 major singles titles.

questions.question: Molla Mallory is remembered for…
questions.explain: Mallory won eight US National singles titles: 1915–18, 1920–22 and 1926.

questions.question: Maureen “Little Mo” Connolly in 1953 became…
choices: The first woman to win a calendar Grand Slam
questions.explain: Calendar Slam at 18: Australia, France, Wimbledon, US. A horseback accident in 1954 ended her career. She is 9–0 in slam finals.

questions.question: Who was the first Black player — man or woman — to win a Grand Slam singles title?
questions.explain: Althea Gibson, 1956 French Championships, over Angela Mortimer. She added Wimbledon and the US Nationals in 1957 and 1958 — five slam singles, 11 slam titles in all.

questions.question: Who publicly pushed the USLTA to accept Althea Gibson at Forest Hills?
questions.explain: Alice Marble’s 1950 American Lawn Tennis magazine letter. Gibson entered the 1950 US Nationals and later won it twice.

questions.question: After tennis, Althea Gibson also became…
choices: The first Black woman on the LPGA tour
questions.explain: Althea Gibson became the first Black woman to join the LPGA Tour in 1964.

questions.question: Who holds the all-time women’s major singles title record in non-wheelchair tennis?
questions.explain: Court won 24 major singles titles: 11 in Australia, five in France, three at Wimbledon and five at the US championships. Serena Williams holds the Open Era women’s record with 23.

questions.question: Margaret Court completed a calendar Grand Slam in…
questions.explain: 1970. The other women’s calendar Slams: Connolly 1953, Graf 1988.

questions.question: Virginia Wade won the first sanctioned Open Era tournament at…
questions.explain: British Hard Court Championships, Bournemouth. She later won the first Open US Open (1968) and Wimbledon in the Jubilee year 1977.

questions.question: The Original 9 signed $1 contracts in 1970 with…
questions.explain: Heldman, publisher of World Tennis, backed by Philip Morris CEO Joe Cullman. First event: Houston Racquet Club, 23 September 1970. Rosie Casals won it.

questions.question: How many players were in the Original 9?
questions.explain: Nine: Billie Jean King, Rosie Casals, Nancy Richey, Peaches Bartkowicz, Valerie Ziegenfuss, Kristy Pigeon, Julie Heldman, Judy Tegart Dalton, Kerry Melville Reid.

questions.question: Which two Original 9 players were Australian?
choices: Judy Tegart Dalton and Kerry Melville Reid
questions.explain: The other seven were American. Julie Heldman was Gladys’s daughter.

questions.question: The WTA was founded in…
questions.explain: Billie Jean King convened ~60 players the week before Wimbledon 1973. Houston 1970 and the Virginia Slims Circuit were the fuse; Gloucester Hotel was the union.

questions.question: First woman athlete to earn $100,000 in a season:
questions.explain: On the inaugural Virginia Slims Circuit. Same year she was already a career-slam hunter.

questions.question: First Grand Slam to offer equal prize money for women and men:
questions.explain: US Open 1973, with the new WTA as leverage. Wimbledon did not match until 2007.

questions.question: The 1973 Battle of the Sexes was…
choices: King vs Riggs in the Houston Astrodome
questions.explain: Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs. Contemporary estimates put the TV audience around 90 million. It was exhibition theater that moved money and attention toward the women’s tour.

questions.question: Billie Jean King’s slam singles total is…
questions.explain: 12: 6 Wimbledon, 4 US, 1 Australia, 1 France. Career slam in singles (completed RG 1972) and mixed. 1973 Wimbledon triple crown: singles, doubles, mixed.

questions.question: Open Era meeting count between Chris Evert and Martina Navratilova:
questions.explain: Evert and Navratilova played 80 times, with Navratilova leading 43–37. Fourteen meetings were major singles finals.

questions.question: Evert and Navratilova finished with how many slam singles each?
questions.explain: Tied on 18. Evert: 7 French, 6 US, 3 Wimbledon, 2 Australia. Martina: 9 Wimbledon, 4 US, 3 Australia, 2 French.

questions.question: Chris Evert’s clay-court winning streak is…
questions.explain: Evert won 125 consecutive clay-court matches from 1973 to 1979. She also won seven Roland Garros singles titles.

questions.question: Most Wimbledon women’s singles titles in the Open Era:
questions.explain: Navratilova 9 (1978–79, 1982–87, 1990). Wills has 8 all-time; Graf and Serena 7 each.

questions.question: Open Era leader in WTA singles titles:
questions.explain: Navratilova 167 singles titles, 8 WTA Finals. She also holds the Open Era doubles mountain.

questions.question: Martina Navratilova defected from Czechoslovakia during…
questions.explain: She stayed in the United States after the 1975 US Open to chase No. 1 without sport-system control.

questions.question: Who is the only non-wheelchair singles player to complete a Calendar Golden Slam?
questions.explain: Steffi Graf won all four women’s singles majors and Olympic singles gold in 1988. Diede de Groot also achieved a calendar Golden Slam in wheelchair singles in 2021.

questions.question: Graf’s 1988 French Open final vs Natasha Zvereva finished…
questions.explain: Graf won the 1988 Roland-Garros final 6–0, 6–0 in about 32 minutes of playing time.

questions.question: Steffi Graf’s slam singles total:
questions.explain: Graf won 22 singles majors: seven Wimbledon, six French, five US and four Australian titles. She is the only non-wheelchair singles player to win each major at least four times.

questions.question: What interrupted Monica Seles’s career for more than two years beginning in 1993?
choices: She was stabbed on court in Hamburg in 1993 and missed more than two years
questions.explain: Seles was attacked on court in Hamburg in 1993. She returned in 1995 and won the 1996 Australian Open, her ninth major singles title.

questions.question: What made Evonne Goolagong Cawley’s 1980 Wimbledon singles title especially significant?
choices: She became the first mother to win it since 1914
questions.explain: Goolagong Cawley won the 1980 Wimbledon singles title as a mother. It was her seventh major singles title.

questions.question: Open Era women’s slam singles record:
questions.explain: Serena 23 (7 Australia, 7 Wimbledon, 6 US, 3 French), 1999–2017. Venus has 7 singles slams, 5 of them Wimbledon.

questions.question: Venus and Serena met in how many slam singles finals?
questions.explain: The sisters met in nine Grand Slam singles finals; Serena won seven. Serena won their four consecutive finals from Roland-Garros 2002 through the Australian Open 2003.

questions.question: A “Serena Slam” means…
choices: Four slams in one calendar year
Holding all four majors at once, not necessarily in one calendar year
Winning Miami and the US Open
questions.explain: Non-calendar slam. She did it twice (2002–03 and 2014–15). Calendar slam still belongs only to Connolly, Court, Graf on the women’s side.

questions.question: Serena’s first slam singles title was…
questions.explain: Serena Williams won her first major singles title at the 1999 US Open, beating Martina Hingis in the final at age 17.

questions.question: Which pair of parents coached Venus and Serena Williams?
choices: Nick Bollettieri and Billie Jean King
questions.explain: Their father Richard Williams and mother Oracene Price coached the sisters. Serena later also worked with Patrick Mouratoglou.

questions.question: Who became the first Asian woman to win a major singles title?
questions.explain: Li Na won Roland Garros in 2011 and the Australian Open in 2014, representing China.

questions.question: Justine Henin’s slam singles total and signature surface:
questions.explain: One-handed backhand, 4 Roland Garros. She never won Wimbledon. Retired the first time in 2008 while still No. 1.

questions.question: Which statement about Kim Clijsters is correct?
choices: Won slams after becoming a mother (US Open 2009, 2010; Australia 2011)
questions.explain: Three slams as a mom plus the 2005 US Open before stepping away.

questions.question: Martina Hingis became WTA No. 1 in 1997 at age…
questions.explain: Hingis became No. 1 on 31 March 1997 at 16 years and 182 days, the youngest player to reach the WTA singles top ranking.

questions.question: Maria Sharapova’s 2004 Wimbledon title came as…
choices: A 17-year-old No. 13 seed defeating Serena Williams
questions.explain: Sharapova beat Serena Williams in the 2004 final to win her first major singles title at age 17.

questions.question: The women’s national team cup is now named…
questions.explain: The ITF renamed Fed Cup the Billie Jean King Cup in 2020.

questions.question: Wightman Cup was…
choices: The women’s World Cup of soccer
A USA–Great Britain women’s team event held from 1923 to 1989
questions.explain: Hazel Wightman founded the competition. It was played annually except during World War II, and ended in 1989.

questions.question: Evert vs Navratilova is the textbook split of…
questions.explain: Evert built her game around baseline consistency, while Navratilova attacked with serve-and-volley tennis. Their contrasting styles made their rivalry distinctive.

questions.question: The last US Open played on grass was…
questions.explain: The US Open used grass through 1974, green clay in 1975–77, and hard courts from 1978. Jimmy Connors won singles titles on all three surfaces.

questions.question: Iga Świątek’s sixth slam singles title was…
questions.explain: Path: RG 2020, 2022–24; US Open 2022; Wimbledon 2025. Four French titles already put her in the Henin/Evert clay conversation.

questions.question: 2025 women’s slam singles champions were…
questions.explain: AO Madison Keys, RG Coco Gauff, Wimbledon Iga Świątek, US Open Aryna Sabalenka.

questions.question: 2026 Australian Open and US Open women’s singles champion:
questions.explain: Rybakina beat Sabalenka in the 2026 AO final (rematch of 2023). She also won the 2026 US Open. 2026 RG: Mirra Andreeva. 2026 Wimbledon: Linda Nosková.

questions.question: Naomi Osaka’s four slams were all on…
choices: Hard courts (2 US Open, 2 Australian Open)
questions.explain: 2018 US, 2019 Australia, 2020 US, 2021 Australia. She has not won RG or Wimbledon.

questions.question: Emma Raducanu’s 2021 US Open is unique because she…
choices: Won a slam as a qualifier, without dropping a set
Won from match point down in every round
questions.explain: Raducanu won the 2021 US Open as a qualifier, winning three qualifying matches and seven main-draw matches without losing a set.

questions.question: Ashleigh Barty’s slam singles titles (3) came at…
choices: France 2019, Wimbledon 2021, Australia 2022 — then she retired at No. 1
questions.explain: Walked away in 2022 while still world No. 1. Career Grand Slam missing only the US Open.

questions.question: Which Chinese player reached the 2024 Australian Open women’s singles final?
choices: Zheng Qinwen (2024 Australian Open final vs Sabalenka)
questions.explain: Zheng Qinwen reached the 2024 Australian Open final against Aryna Sabalenka and later won singles gold at the Paris Olympics.

questions.question: How many Grand Slam singles finals did Chris Evert reach?
questions.explain: Chris Evert reached 34 major singles finals and won 18. She reached at least the semifinals at 52 of her 56 major appearances.

questions.question: Through the 2026 US Open, who holds the Open Era women’s record for Grand Slam singles match wins?
questions.explain: Serena Williams leads the official WTA Open Era table with 367 wins. Martina Navratilova has 306 and Chris Evert 299.

questions.question: Who won the US Nationals eight times before it was even the Open?
questions.explain: Mallory 8. Wills 7 US. Court’s 5 US include Open Era.

questions.question: Maria Bueno of Brazil’s slam singles haul:
questions.explain: Maria Bueno won three Wimbledon and four US singles championships, all before the Open Era.

questions.question: Dorothea Lambert Chambers is mostly a…
choices: A seven-time Wimbledon singles champion between 1903 and 1914
questions.explain: Dorothea Lambert Chambers won seven Wimbledon singles titles between 1903 and 1914.

questions.question: Which women-only professional circuit grew from the Original 9’s 1970 Houston breakaway?
questions.explain: The Virginia Slims Circuit expanded in 1971 and helped lay the foundations for the WTA, founded in 1973.

questions.question: Who was the first president of the WTA?
questions.explain: King, 1973. Heldman built the circuit but was the promoter, not the elected player president.

questions.question: Which woman completed a career Golden Slam in singles by winning Olympic gold in 2012?
questions.explain: Serena Williams completed the career Golden Slam with Olympic singles gold at London 2012. Venus has won Wimbledon and the US Open in singles, but neither the Australian Open nor Roland-Garros.

questions.question: World TeamTennis, launched 1974, mattered to women’s history because…
choices: It mixed men and women on the same teams and paid them as professionals in the US summer
questions.explain: King was a founder. Billie Jean and the original WTT teams normalized co-ed pro tennis in American arenas.

questions.question: “The Original 9” refers to…
choices: The nine players who broke away to start a women’s pro circuit in 1970
questions.explain: Houston, $1 contracts, Virginia Slims. Without them there is no modern WTA prize-money ladder.

questions.question: Tracy Austin won the 1979 US Open at 16 years 9 months. That record for youngest US Open women’s champion…
questions.explain: Austin also won 1981. A back injury truncated the career. Hingis was younger at other slams, not the US Open.

questions.question: Which set of women’s tennis firsts is correct?
choices: Althea Gibson: first Black major singles champion; Billie Jean King: first WTA president; Li Na: first Asian woman major singles champion
Naomi Osaka: first Black major champion; Chris Evert: first WTA president
Margaret Court: first Black major champion
Virginia Wade: first Asian major champion
questions.explain: Gibson broke the major singles barrier in 1956; King became the WTA’s first president in 1973; Li Na won Roland Garros in 2011.

questions.question: Coco Gauff’s first two slam singles titles:
questions.explain: 2019 Wimbledon was a 15-year-old run to the fourth round over Venus, not a title.

questions.question: The phrase “women’s prize money is a fraction of the men’s” at the 1970 Pacific Southwest led directly to…
choices: The Houston breakaway and Virginia Slims Circuit
questions.explain: The large prize-money disparity at the Pacific Southwest event helped spur the Original 9’s breakaway. Gladys Heldman organized the Houston tournament that led to the Virginia Slims Circuit.

questions.question: Who holds the Open Era record for most consecutive Wimbledon women’s titles?
questions.explain: Six straight. Lenglen won five in a row in the amateur era (1919–23).

questions.question: Which is the correct slam-singles order, most to fewer?
questions.explain: Commit that ladder. Everything else in women’s slam arguments hangs off it.

questions.question: Margaret Court’s combined major haul (singles + doubles + mixed) is…
questions.explain: Court won 64 major titles: 24 singles, 19 women’s doubles and 21 mixed doubles. This count includes shared Australian mixed doubles titles in 1965 and 1969.

questions.question: Martina Navratilova’s Open Era major total across all three disciplines:
questions.explain: 18 singles + 31 women’s doubles + 10 mixed = 59. Open Era record. Court’s 64 is the all-time mark including amateur years.

questions.question: Most women’s doubles slam titles, one player:
questions.explain: Navratilova 31. Next all-time cluster: Brough, duPont, and Shriver on 21; Court 19; Zvereva 18.

questions.question: How many women’s doubles Grand Slam titles did Martina Navratilova and Pam Shriver win as a team?
questions.explain: They won 20 majors as a team, including all four in 1984. They won eight consecutive majors from Wimbledon 1983 through Roland-Garros 1985.

questions.question: A “boxed set” in tennis means…
choices: Winning singles, doubles, and mixed at all four majors over a career
questions.explain: Court did it twice. Navratilova completed hers when she added mixed Australia 2003 with Leander Paes at age 46.

questions.question: Which woman completed the 1963 mixed doubles calendar Grand Slam with Ken Fletcher?
questions.explain: Margaret Court, then Margaret Smith, and Ken Fletcher won all four mixed doubles majors in 1963. Owen Davidson also completed a mixed doubles calendar Grand Slam in 1967.

questions.question: Most mixed-doubles slam titles, women:
questions.explain: Court 21. Hart 15, King 11, duPont 10, Navratilova 10.

questions.question: Who won the 2006 US Open mixed doubles title at age 49?
questions.explain: Navratilova won with Bob Bryan. It was her 10th major mixed doubles title; she also won 31 major women’s doubles titles. Her first major title was the 1974 French Open mixed doubles with Iván Molina.

questions.question: Venus and Serena’s slam doubles titles as a pair:
questions.explain: 14 majors together — tied with Fernández/Zvereva for second-most by an Open Era team. They also have Olympic gold as a team (Career Golden Slam).

questions.question: Only pairing to win a calendar-year women’s doubles Grand Slam:
questions.explain: Bueno (1960) and Hingis (1998) did a doubles Slam with more than one partner in the same year. The intact pair Slam is Navratilova–Shriver only.

questions.question: Open Era WTA doubles titles leader:
questions.explain: The WTA’s 2026 record book lists Navratilova first with 177 doubles titles. She also won 167 singles titles.

questions.question: A Triple Crown is…
choices: Singles, doubles, and mixed at the same major in the same year
questions.explain: Martina Navratilova achieved this at the 1987 US Open by winning women’s singles, women’s doubles, and mixed doubles.

questions.question: How many women’s doubles major titles did Louise Brough and Margaret Osborne duPont each win?
questions.explain: Brough and duPont each won 21 women’s doubles majors. They won 20 major titles together.

questions.question: How many major titles did Elizabeth Ryan win in women’s doubles?
questions.explain: Ryan won 17 women’s doubles majors and nine mixed doubles majors, for 26 in total. Her 19 Wimbledon titles combined women’s doubles and mixed doubles.

questions.question: Gigi Fernández and Natasha Zvereva’s slam doubles total as a team:
questions.explain: Fernández and Zvereva won 14 women’s doubles majors together. Zvereva won 18 individually; Navratilova won 31 and Shriver 21 in the Open Era.

questions.question: Navratilova and Shriver’s documented doubles winning streak:
questions.explain: Navratilova and Shriver won 109 consecutive doubles matches in the 1980s.

questions.question: Martina Hingis’s later-career second act was mostly…
choices: Doubles and mixed — she added a stack of slams after her singles peak, including mixed with Paes and Mirza doubles years
questions.explain: Hingis has 13 women’s doubles slams plus 7 mixed. The 1998 doubles Slam used more than one partner.

questions.question: Krejčíková / Siniaková are the modern pair associated with…
choices: Career Super Slam as a doubles team (all four majors + Olympic gold + year-end championship)
questions.explain: Krejčíková and Siniaková won all four women’s doubles majors, Olympic doubles gold in Tokyo, and the 2021 WTA Finals together. Krejčíková also won singles titles at Roland-Garros 2021 and Wimbledon 2024.

questions.question: Rosie Casals belongs in a doubles IQ set because…
choices: Original 9 ringleader with King, Wimbledon/US doubles staple, 112 WTA doubles titles

questions.question: In doubles, what do “deuce court” and “ad court” mean?
choices: The right-hand and left-hand halves respectively, viewed from each player’s own end facing the net
questions.explain: Deuce is the right half and ad is the left half from your own end facing the net. “I-formation” names a doubles formation, not a court. Break points can be played on either half.

questions.question: May a doubles team switch its receiving order at the start of a new set?
choices: Yes. Serving order in a set is locked once chosen; receiving order may be changed at the start of a new set
questions.explain: ITF Rules 14–15 permit new serving and receiving orders at the start of a new set. During a set, the chosen orders remain in force. Rule 27 separately governs errors; a receiving-order error continues for the rest of that game and is corrected for the next receiving game.

questions.question: Who completed a Career Golden Slam in women’s doubles as a team first?
questions.explain: Venus and Serena Williams completed their career Golden Slam in women’s doubles together at the 2001 Australian Open, after winning Olympic doubles gold in 2000.

questions.question: Navratilova’s last match as a player was…
choices: Winning 2006 US Open mixed with Bob Bryan, then retiring
questions.explain: Walked off with a major. That is the correct ending for that career.

questions.question: Court’s mixed slam count vs her women’s doubles slam count:
questions.explain: The 64 breaks 24 / 19 / 21. Mixed is the quiet third of the record people skip.

questions.question: What’s the call: opponent’s ball lands on the line. You saw chalk fly.
choices: In. Any part of the ball touching the line is good
questions.explain: The Code §7 / ITF. A ball 99% out is 100% good. Chalk can fly when the ball hits the line.

questions.question: What’s the call: long rally, you didn’t see the ball land. Opponent says “not sure, let’s play a let.”
choices: No. A ball that cannot be called out is good. You do not get a let for not seeing it
questions.explain: The Code §8. The “I’m not sure, play a let” after a clean winner is the most infuriating sentence in rec tennis, and it is wrong.

questions.question: What’s the call: you call it out, then see the mark is good.
choices: Reverse it. Opponent wins the point — no replay
Always a let after a reversed call
questions.explain: The Code §12. Exception: reverse a fault call on a serve that hit the net, and the server gets two serves.

questions.question: What’s the call: doubles. You called it out; your partner says it was good.
choices: Good. Give opponents the call that helps them
questions.explain: The Code §14. Partner feelings lose to opponents’ benefit of the doubt.

questions.question: What’s the call: a ball from the next court rolls on. You smash the sitter anyway, miss long, then yell “let!”
choices: Let — the ball was on the court
No let. You chose to play it. Two-chance option is dead
questions.explain: The Code §17. Prompt calls. Play the ball and you bought the result.

questions.question: What’s the call: the ball hits you in the chest before bouncing. You were standing three feet behind the baseline.
choices: In, you were out of the court
You lose the point wherever you are standing
Only lose it inside the lines
questions.explain: The Code §19 and §43. Catching or being hit by a ball in play = point over.

questions.question: What’s the call: unofficiated match. Server is foot-faulting every first serve. You have not warned them.
choices: Warn first, try to get an official, then call only flagrant faults you can see from your side
Never call foot faults in rec tennis
questions.explain: The Code §24. Touching the line is still a foot fault (§23). Enforcement without a chair is tightly limited so the match does not become a referee war.

questions.question: What’s the call: first serve looks long to the serving team. Receiver plays it and nets the return.
choices: Serving team may now call the fault
questions.explain: The Code §26 exception. Serving team generally stays quiet on first serves. If the receiver plays a fault and does not put it in play, the serving team may call it.

questions.question: What’s the call: you take a full cut at a “quick” serve and miss. Then you say you weren’t ready.
choices: You were ready. Swinging means ready
questions.explain: The Code §29. Receiver plays to the server’s reasonable pace. Attempted return = presumed ready.

questions.question: What’s the call: between first and second serve a ball rolls on. You spend 20 seconds kicking it aside. Server wants two serves.
choices: Not automatically. Brief clearing is not an interruption. Receiver judges whether the delay was long enough
questions.explain: The Code §30. Interrupted second-serve motion = two serves. Casual tidy-up between serves ≠ two serves.

questions.question: What’s the call: server caused the delay between first and second serve (untied a shoe, argued a call).
questions.explain: The Code §30. Server’s fault → one serve. Receiver or outside interference → two.

questions.question: What’s the call: doubles. You yell “switch!” while the ball is going toward the other team, and they miss.
choices: If the yell hindered them and they stop in time, they can take the point as deliberate hindrance. If they play on and miss, they lost the claim
Only the chair can hear talking
questions.explain: The Code §34. Talk when the ball is coming to you. Do not talk when it is going the other way.

questions.question: What’s the call: opponent’s phone rings mid-point.
choices: You may stop immediately and claim the point — ringing phone is a deliberate hindrance
questions.explain: The Code §36.

questions.question: What’s the call: your racket flies out of your hand and hits the net while the ball is in play.
choices: You lose the point. Something in your control is not a let. Also: touching the net with the racket while the ball is in play loses the point
questions.explain: ITF Rule 24(g): a racket touching the net while the ball is in play loses the point, even when dropped. The Code §36 separately says a dropped racket or shoe is not grounds for a let.

questions.question: What’s the call: opponent’s hat falls off mid-point and it puts you off.
choices: You may immediately call a let (unintentional hindrance). They may not claim a let for their own hat
questions.explain: The Code §36.

questions.question: What’s the call: opponent is grunting so loud you cannot hear the ball. There is no official.
choices: Seek an official; only an official may rule grunting a hindrance and apply the appropriate remedy
questions.explain: The Code §37 reserves this ruling to officials. A let or loss of point depends on whether the offending player has already been warned.

questions.question: What’s the call: clay. The mark touches the line with a sliver of the ball print.
choices: Good. Any part of the mark on the line is in. Opponent does not cross the net to inspect
questions.explain: The Code §21. You are not required to show the mark.

questions.question: What’s the call: you reach over the net and volley the ball before it has crossed.
questions.explain: The Code §19 / ITF. The ball must cross to your side first.

questions.question: What’s the call: towel draped over the net during the point.
choices: Fine if it is your towel
Never put towels or clothes on the net. Towels go on the ground outside the net post or at the back fence
ITF requires towels on the net
questions.explain: The Code §46.

questions.question: What’s the call: after the match you shake hands, then remember the net was two inches high the whole time.
choices: The match is over. Handshake acknowledges it. Points played in good faith stood even if the net was wrong
questions.explain: The Code §2.

questions.question: What’s the call: you and your opponent disagree about the score but agree on some points. Which method should you try first?
choices: Count every point you both agree on; replay only the disputed point or game. Coin toss if you cannot agree who served
questions.explain: The Code §32 first counts agreed points and games and replays disputed ones. Next try a mutually agreeable score; finally use a racket spin or coin toss. A coin toss can also resolve disputed service order or the court for a replayed point.

questions.question: What’s the call: spectator yells “out!” You stopped. The ball was in.
choices: Spectator calls are not hindrances. Play on — or you just gifted the point by stopping
questions.explain: The Code §16 and §36. Spectators never make calls. Their noise is not a let.

questions.question: What’s the call: first serve into the net sits in the middle of the box. Returner does not move it. Server wants it cleared before second serve.
choices: When the ball is not in play, honor a reasonable request to remove a ball on the court
Must wait until the game ends
questions.explain: The Code §42. Distant balls wait until the end of a game. A ball sitting in the service box is not distant.

questions.question: What’s the call: you catch a lob that was sailing three feet long, before it bounces, standing on the next court.
choices: Your point — it was going out
You lose the point. Catching a ball in play before the bounce loses it, anywhere
questions.explain: The Code §43. Let it bounce. Then call it.

questions.question: What’s the call: you ask the opponent “was that out?” They say “it was good.”
choices: You must accept that opinion. If neither of you has an opinion, the ball is good
questions.explain: The Code §11. You only request help on a call that ended the point.

questions.question: What’s the call: warm-up has already run 12 minutes. Opponent wants more serves.
choices: Warm-up is 5–10 minutes, not practice. Take warm-up serves before the first serve of the match
questions.explain: The Code §3–4. Decline to warm the opponent up and you forfeit your own warm-up.

questions.question: What’s the call: server’s second-serve toss is up when a ball rolls on and they catch the toss.
choices: Two serves — the second-serve motion was interrupted by a ball coming on court
questions.explain: The Code §30 first sentence.

questions.question: What’s the call: you clearly see your own first serve was long. Opponent says nothing and the ball sits.
choices: Must call it out — all serves
You are not required to call your own first serve out. You should call your own shots out except on first serve
Automatic fault only if they ask
questions.explain: The Code §13 exception for first serve.

questions.question: What’s the call: changeover has already eaten two and a half minutes. Opponent is still re-taping a blister and talking.
choices: Stalling. Odd-game changeover is 90 seconds; set break is 2 minutes. Get an official. Point Penalty System applies
questions.explain: The Code §40. Also stalling: one-third pace, starting an argument to rest, clearing a first serve that does not need clearing, excessive bouncing.

questions.question: What’s the call: underhand serve, legal toss, hits the box.
choices: Legal. The serve must be struck before the ball hits the ground; underhand is allowed
questions.explain: ITF / USTA. People hate it. It is still in.

questions.question: Wheelchair tennis allows…
questions.explain: ITF Wheelchair Tennis Rules. Quad division has extra classification rules.

questions.question: Best-of-three sets means…
questions.explain: Best-of-three means the first player to win two sets wins the match. Grand Slam women’s singles main draws use this format; men’s singles main draws use best-of-five.

questions.question: Men’s singles main-draw matches at Grand Slam tournaments are played in which format?
questions.explain: Final-set rules have varied (advantage set vs 10-point tiebreak). Know the event year.

questions.question: In Wimbledon singles main draws, what happens at 6–6 in the deciding set under the format introduced in 2022?
choices: A 10-point tiebreak at 6–6 in the final set
questions.explain: A first-to-10, win-by-two tiebreak decides the match.

questions.question: Under the standard service-let rule, a serve clips the net and lands in the correct service box. What is the call?
questions.explain: Lets exist on first and second serves. A let on second is still second serve.

questions.question: Serve hits the net and goes out of the box.
questions.explain: Let only if the ball would have been in.

questions.question: Ball hits the net and drops in on a rally (not a serve).
choices: Play on — winner if they cannot reach it
questions.explain: Net-cord winners are legal in a rally.

questions.question: During a standard serve, the server’s feet must not touch the baseline or court until…
questions.explain: ITF Rule 18 prohibits touching the baseline or court during the service motion. The server may jump and be airborne over the line before contact.

questions.question: During a serve the server’s foot may…
choices: Not touch the baseline or the court before contact; it may be in the air over the line
Rest on the line if only the toe
Step in early if it is a second serve
questions.explain: Air over the line is fine. Touch is not.

questions.question: Order of serve in a 7-point tiebreak: the first server serves…
choices: One point, then partners/players serve two points each
questions.explain: Then change ends every six points.

questions.question: Who serves first in a match is decided by…
choices: A toss / spin. Winner may serve or receive or pick the end
questions.explain: ITF 9.

questions.question: After an odd-numbered game, players…
questions.explain: 1, 3, 5… and in a tiebreak after every 6 points.

questions.question: In doubles, a rally ball hits a net post and then lands in the opponents’ court. What is the call?
questions.explain: ITF Rule 25 permits this return in doubles. In singles played with a doubles net and singles sticks, the outside net posts are permanent fixtures: hitting them before the ball lands loses the point.

questions.question: Your shot hits a roof or an overhead camera before it bounces in the opponent’s court. What is the result?
choices: Point to the opponent of the player who hit it (permanent fixture out of play)
questions.explain: Under ITF Rules 2 and 13, touching a permanent fixture before the ball lands loses the point. If a ball first bounces in the correct court and then touches a permanent fixture, the striker wins the point.
